method: The page treats a transfer rate as a quantity per second expressed in a unit of data and converts every unit through bits per second. One byte is eight bits, so a byte unit is eight times its bit equivalent at the same prefix: 100 Mbit/s is 12.5 MB/s and 1 kB/s is 8 kbit/s. Decimal SI prefixes step by powers of 1,000 (kbit/s, Mbit/s, Gbit/s, Tbit/s and kB/s through TB/s) and binary IEC prefixes step by powers of 1,024 (KiB/s, MiB/s, GiB/s, TiB/s), so 1 MiB/s is 1,048.576 kB/s and 1 GiB/s is 1,073.741824 MB/s. The chosen pair is the headline result and every supported unit is listed in a grouped table, which keeps both families visible at once. Results are rounded to six significant digits and grouped in thousands; values below 0.0001 or at least 1e13 are printed in exponent form so that 1 bit/s does not collapse to zero in TiB/s. Input is a plain decimal number, optionally grouped with commas, from zero up to 1 Pbit/s (1e15 bit/s) in the chosen unit; text, exponent notation, a misplaced comma and negative values are refused with a specific message rather than clipped. This is nominal unit arithmetic only: it does not model protocol headers, framing, forward error correction, retransmission, duplex asymmetry or measured goodput, so a real link carries less payload than its line rate, and the decimal-versus-binary distinction reflects how a network rate is quoted against how an operating system reports file throughput. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.
